title: Number of Self-Divisible Permutations
statement:
Given an integer `n`, look at the permutations of the numbers `1, 2, ..., n`, written as 1-indexed arrays `a`. Call a permutation self-divisible when every position is coprime with the value placed there: `gcd(a[i], i) == 1` for each `1 <= i <= n`.

Return how many permutations of `1..n` are self-divisible.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying all `n!` orders is too slow at `n = 12` (about 479 million). But when filling positions from left to right, the only thing that matters for the future is **which values are already used**, not their order: the next position is always one more than the number of values placed. A bitmask of used values therefore describes the state completely, and there are only `2^n` of them.

## Approach

1. Let `dp[mask]` be the number of ways to fill positions `1..k` using exactly the values in `mask`, where `k` is the number of set bits. Start with `dp[0] = 1`.
2. Process masks in increasing order; adding a value always makes the mask bigger, so every state is complete before it is used.
3. For each mask, `placed[mask]` counts its set bits, so the next `position` is `placed[mask] + 1`.
4. For every unused `value` with `gcd(value, position) === 1`, add `dp[mask]` to `dp[mask | bit]`.
5. The answer is `dp[full]`, where every value has been placed.

## Example 1, step by step

With `n = 1`, `full = 1` and `dp = [1, 0]`. At `mask = 0`, `position = 1`; value 1 is unused and `gcd(1, 1) = 1`, so `dp[1]` becomes 1. The answer is `dp[full] = 1`.

For a richer picture take `n = 3`. Position 1 accepts every value, so each one-value mask gets 1. Position 2 rejects value 2, giving `dp[{1,3}] = 2`, `dp[{1,2}] = 1` (2 then 1) and `dp[{2,3}] = 1` (2 then 3). Position 3 rejects value 3, so `dp[full]` collects 2 from `{1,3}` and 1 from `{2,3}`: the answer is 3.

## Complexity

- Time: O(2ⁿ · n · log n): each mask tries every value and runs a short gcd.
- Space: O(2ⁿ) for `dp` and `placed`.

## Pitfalls

- Positions are 1-based: position `i` and value `i` share the factor `i`, so only position 1 can hold its own value.
- `gcd(1, x) = 1`, so value 1 fits every position and position 1 accepts every value.
- The position comes from the number of used values, not from the highest bit of `mask`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `full` | mask with all `n` values used |
| `dp` | ways to reach each set of used values |
| `placed` | number of values in each mask |
| `mask` | values used so far |
| `position` | the next 1-based index to fill |
| `value`, `bit` | the candidate value and its mask bit |

narration.2: Euclid's algorithm: two numbers are coprime when their gcd is 1.
narration.3: The mask with all n values used; bit v - 1 stands for value v.
narration.4: dp[mask] counts the ways to fill the first positions with exactly the values in mask.
narration.6: Before anything is placed there is exactly one (empty) arrangement.
narration.8: Visit masks in increasing order; adding a value always leads to a larger mask.
narration.9: The number of used values equals the bits of mask >> 1 plus its lowest bit.
narration.10: No arrangement reaches this set of values, so there is nothing to extend.
narration.13: With k values placed, the next value goes to position k + 1.
narration.14: Try every value as the occupant of that position.
narration.16: It must still be unused and share no factor with the position.
narration.17: Every arrangement of mask extends to one of mask | bit.
narration.21: Every value placed: this counts the self-divisible permutations.
